requirements: Portable public APIs and policy live in canonical .atto source; backend copies must match exact bytes.
Transport implementation may call per-backend native TLS, QUIC, UDP, and OS/event-loop primitives; no .java standard library implementation.
In browser WASM, raw UDP sockets are unavailable; use browser-exposed networking capabilities and fail closed for missing features.
Do not report an actual HTTP/3 implementation on the strength of policy functions or source-byte parity alone.
Only advertise h3 after successful QUIC/TLS negotiation and HTTP/3 SETTINGS, ALPN h3, peer certificate validation, and required feature negotiation.
HTTP/3 to TCP HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 fallback is opt-in/allowed by policy, never silently downgrade when require_http3 is set.
QUIC datagrams are unreliable and must be bounded by negotiated peer limit, path MTU, actor memory budgets and permissions.
Zero-RTT requires explicit opt-in and replay-safe request handling; do not automatically replay unsafe requests.
Actor-owned buffers and logical stacks cannot escape their owner, suspend across unpinned loans, or be used after close.
Cancellation and deadlines must propagate to streams and I/O; backpressure controls both connection and actor mailboxes.
All socket and TLS operations exposed to Atto guest code must be nonblocking; blocking wrapper names must end in _blocking.
Guest compilation, executable AOT artifacts, interop tests, and workload benchmarks need independent per-backend CI evidence.
acceptance: Canonical and backend source-file Git blob identity at pinned heads
RS compiler executes .atto smoke guest exit 42 and rejects invalid source
Independent LLVM, Java/Graal, .NET NativeAOT, RS, and WASM guest executions
TLS 1.3/ALPN h3, cert rejection, UDP-blocked fallback and require-h3 no-fallback tests
Actor teardown and 100K+ request/connection cycles with memory and GC measurements
External h3/QUIC implementation interop and benchmarks against h2/h1 using same workload
